node.label: Audra Simpson
node.date_label: “On Ethnographic Refusal” 2007 · Mohawk Interruptus 2014 · “The Ruse of Consent” 2017
node.description: An anthropologist of Kahnawà:ke Mohawk nationhood whose method has become a resource for historians. In 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) she proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' from Iroquois studies, which since Morgan had sought 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them', and she made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in'. History-writing, she argued, 'naturalises this occupation'; her own analysis reaches back through colonial membership law. Indigenous contexts are 'never properly "post-colonial"'. Mohawk Interruptus (2014), as Nicoll's review quotes it, carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's migrations and into Morgan and Parker's ethnology, which became 'a regulatory body of knowledge' used 'to adjudicate claims to land'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Audra Simpson; 'Paths Toward a Mohawk Nation' (2001); 'To the Reserve and Back Again' (PhD, McGill, 2003); 'On the Logic of Discernment' (2007); 'On Ethnographic Refusal: Indigeneity, "Voice" and Colonial Citizenship' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus: Political Life Across the Borders of Settler States (2014); 'The Ruse of Consent and the Anatomy of "Refusal"' (2017).
node.scope_note: Read in full: 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007). Mohawk Interruptus (2014) is known through Nicoll's review essay (2015), which quotes it with page numbers, and through the Duke page; 'The Ruse of Consent' (2017) at abstract level. In the texts read she does not criticise Wolfe; he appears only as a supporting citation (2007, n. 3). In Canadian History PhDs: 34 citing theses; share 0.3% in 2000–09 and 4.1% in 2018–25 (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).

proposed_edges.relationship: Makes refusal a method: sovereignty 'matters at the level of method and representation', and ethnography becomes a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007, read in full), p. 72 for both quotations; p. 78: refusals 'tell us when to stop' and 'critique and move us away from statist forms of recognition'; p. 75: a foreign culture 'naturalises this occupation through history-writing and the very analytics that are used to know them'. Her own analysis reaches back through colonial membership law (pp. 72–76); interview passages are not used. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Criticises Iroquois studies since Morgan as 'a documentary form' seeking 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them', producing 'anthropologies of timeless, procedural "tradition"' at odds with Six Nations sovereignty (2007)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, pp. 70–71 (Morgan's League 'a paradigmatic text of reconstructed and salvage ethnography'). Nicoll's review essay (2015, read in full) quotes Mohawk Interruptus p. 93: the Morgan–Parker tradition became 'a regulatory body of knowledge' in a state 'that uses anthropological and historical archives to determine legal presence, to adjudicate claims to land'; the book is known through that reader only. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Reads Kahnawà:ke membership disputes as carrying 'the punctuating, juridical bestowals of settler colonialism', with status designations inscribed on persons (2007); refusal as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society' (2017)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74; 2017 abstract (existing source, read). Nicoll (2015) quotes Mohawk Interruptus p. 3 on 'the structure of settlement that strangles their political form'. Wolfe appears in the 2007 article only as a supporting citation (n. 3); no critique of Wolfe is implied. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Finds at Kahnawà:ke no 'doubleness' of colonised consciousness of the kind 'that Fanon, Bhabha and Giddens speak of', but 'a tripleness, a quadrupleness' revealed at the point of refusal (2007)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74. Nicoll (2015, p. 56, read) independently reports that 'Simpson distinguishes this refusal from Fanonian "double consciousness"'. A qualified critique of one concept, not of Fanon's work as a whole. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Indigenous contexts are 'never properly "post-colonial"'; the refusals she recorded found no 'neat placement … within post-colonial studies or analysis' (2007)
Simpson builds her account of Morgan's ethnology as an outgrowth of 'play' as an Indian on Deloria's Playing Indian (2007)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2007, p. 71 and n. 16 (Deloria, Playing Indian, 1998). A citation-level resource; held for stage 2 unless the coordinator accepts citation-level resource edges. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's own open-access PDF, pp. 67–80 and notes 1–28 (footer 'Junctures, 9, Dec 2007'). Passages used: 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' (pp. 70–71); Iroquois studies 'a documentary form' seeking 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them' (p. 71); refusal as 'a calculus … of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (p. 72); 'never properly "post-colonial"' (p. 68); no doubleness 'that Fanon, Bhabha and Giddens speak of' (p. 74); 'the punctuating, juridical bestowals of settler colonialism' (p. 74); history-writing 'naturalises this occupation' (p. 75); credits Moreton-Robinson (p. 69) and Alfred's books (p. 78 n. 28). Interview passages are not used (OCAP limits). Wolfe appears only as a supporting citation (n. 3). Author note: assistant professor, Cornell (p. 80).

row.context: Anthropologist who moved 'away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method of research and writing; Mohawk Interruptus (2014) is known through Nicoll's review.
